prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, reaching unprecedented accuracy and stability in the measurement of time

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are a concrete, well-bounded invention with a clean two-person credit boundary: Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and first realisation, and Ye's carrying of the strontium lattice clock to fractional uncertainties near 1e-18, with record clock-comparison and many-body measurements. Many independent laboratories have reproduced and surpassed the performance, the physics is stable, and the clocks now outperform the caesium definition of the second while the redefinition is still pending, so timing is good. The work rests on atomic structure (differential light shifts, magic wavelengths, blackbody and relativistic corrections), laser cooling and comb metrology, and it enables relativistic geodesy and searches for variation of constants. Four of eight colleagues ranked it in the top four, and it is one of the few shortlisted candidates where neither attribution nor maturity is seriously in doubt.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is novelty and framing. The 2005 prize (frequency combs) and the 2012 prize (ion control) already cover adjacent precision-measurement territory, and single-ion optical clocks, including Al+ clocks, are not credited here. The achievement is also metrological, an improvement in accuracy rather than a new phenomenon, so some colleagues will see it as technology. On raw opening support, B047 has more top-three placements (four against three) and B051 a higher Borda total, so the committee could reasonably prefer a candidate with broader appeal across subfields.

responses.point: Ranked B010 first as a decisive advance in what can be measured and how accurately, reaching 1e-18, with the pair Katori and Ye as the natural credit and the redefinition of the second not yet done.
responses.response: I agree on the merits and on the two-name credit. I would qualify the claim that the prize story is purely about accuracy. The case is stronger if the citation rests on the magic-wavelength concept, which is what allows many atoms to be interrogated without perturbing the transition. That separates it from ion clocks and from the comb work of 2005. I do not think the pending redefinition is a risk, since the science is already settled. Your own concern about ion clocks being part of the same story is real, and I think it argues for a citation that names the lattice scheme specifically.

responses.point: Ranked B047 first because the Z2 invariant, not a broken symmetry, classifies insulators, and called recognition overdue, while placing B010 sixth with attention to overlap with comb and clock prizes.
responses.response: I take the conceptual depth of B047 seriously, and I ranked it second myself, partly because of the spin-orbit physics I know from relativistic atomic structure. My difficulty is attribution. A three-person cap leaves out Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, who proposed the HgTe route, and the 3D experimenters, so any trio is contestable. The 2016 topological prize also adds an overlap question you raised yourself. On the comb overlap for B010, the 2005 award recognised a different contribution, the comb as a ruler. The lattice clock is a distinct achievement that uses it, so I would not treat that overlap as disqualifying.

responses.point: Ranked B041 first and B010 eighth, calling the lattice clock a clear, original invention but raising overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes and whether technological emphasis outweighs new physics.
responses.response: I take the point on technological emphasis, but I would answer that the clocks have produced physics results: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, bounds on variation of constants and clock-comparison tests. On B041, I share your concern about a return to superconducting circuits so soon after 2025, and the omission of Girvin and Huang from the trio adds an attribution problem. That is why I ranked it seventh. I would put B041 below B010 on both timing and credit cleanliness.

responses.point: Ranked B061 first for the IceCube observational window, and ranked B010 fourth, noting that the diffuse flux is confirmed in several channels but rests on one experiment, and that credit among three named people and early pioneers is a judgement.
responses.response: IceCube is a real discovery of nature, and I ranked it sixth, so we differ on weight rather than on merit. My reservation is the one you state: confirmation comes largely from a single collaboration of hundreds, and the credit among Halzen, Karle, Spiering and the DUMAND, Baikal and AMANDA pioneers cannot be cleanly settled with three names. A lattice clock candidate has the opposite profile, with independent confirmation by several laboratories and a clean two-name boundary. I accept that you would weigh the novelty of a new observational window more heavily than I do.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat optical lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize.
Whether a precision-measurement invention can command a majority against candidates with a larger first-place or top-three count such as B047 and B051.
Relative weight of Katori's proposal versus Ye's accuracy milestones, and whether single-ion optical clocks should be recognised in the same citation, which the credited names do not allow.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for B010, B047 or B046. My documented collaborations (L'Huillier, Keller, Schuch, Dahlstrom, Argenti, Indelicato) do not involve the credited names of any shortlisted candidate. Without a documented tie, I note only that clock physics is close to my field of atomic structure.
